tagline.text: A secluded camping cove of volcanic-ash sand ringed by green mountains

children.text: A broad cove reachable only by boat from the Zambales coast at San Antonio, where gray sand formed from Mount Pinatubo's ash meets agoho forest and green mountain ridges. Quieter than neighboring Anawangin, it's a good spot for peaceful beach camping and waterfall trekking.
Nagsasa Cove is a bay reached from the fishing village of Pundaquit in San Antonio, Zambales, about
45 minutes–1 hour

south along the coast by banca (outrigger boat). With no road access, you can only get there by boat, and grassy mountain ridges wrap around it like a screen, giving a sense of being cut off from the outside world the moment you arrive.
The sand here is said to have built up as ash from the

eruption of Mount Pinatubo washed down the rivers and settled. That's why the sand isn't white but a silvery gray, and behind the beach grows a forest of agoho (Casuarina) trees with their drooping needle-like leaves. A freshwater stream flowing down from the mountains meets the sea at the beach's southern end, forming a calm lagoon — photographers love the mountain reflections on its surface in the morning.

Nagsasa has a wider beach and fewer people than nearby Anawangin Cove, being farther out. Several families and local residents share management of the campsites, some run by Aeta community members who settled in the area after the Pinatubo eruption. There's almost no electricity or phone signal, and amenities amount to little more than restrooms, showers, and a small shop.

It suits groups of camping-loving friends or club members, couples wanting to avoid crowded beaches, and travelers who want to put their phones down and unwind. If you'd rather stay somewhere comfortable, it's worth staying in Pundaquit and visiting as a day-trip hop instead.

Pitching a tent in the shade of the agoho forest behind the beach and spending the night to the sound of waves is the heart of a Nagsasa trip. With no light pollution, the Milky Way is sometimes visible on a clear night.
Follow the stream inland from the beach for about
30 minutes–1 hour
and you'll reach a small waterfall and pool. The path branches in several places, so go with a local guide — water flow is highest just after the wet season.
Head out to the lagoon before the sun climbs over the mountains and the ridgeline and agoho forest mirror perfectly on the still water. Early morning, when the wind is calmest, is best.
A
20–30 minute
climb up the grassy hill on one side of the beach reveals the crescent-shaped cove, gray sand, and sea all at once. There's no shade, so climb in the morning or at sunset.

blocks.title: Island hopping to Capones and Camara Islands

children.text: A popular hopping package stops at Capones Island, with a lighthouse from the late Spanish era, and Camara Island, where a sandbar appears at low tide, along the way. Some islands are skipped if the waves are high.

blocks.title: A sunset walk on the beach

children.text: Since the sun sets over the sea at the mouth of the cove, you can watch the sunset from anywhere on the beach. Walk slowly from one end of the sand to the other and take in the sea and mountains turning red.

blocks.title: Comparing the two coves with Anawangin

children.text: Spend the night at quiet Nagsasa, then stop briefly at Anawangin on your way back. Both have the same volcanic-ash sand and agoho forest, but Anawangin feels cozy and lively while Nagsasa is broad and calm — it's fun to feel the difference in mood between the two.

From the Victory Liner terminal in Cubao, Pasay, or Caloocan, Manila, take a bus bound for Iba or Santa Cruz, Zambales, and get off in San Antonio. It takes about
4–5 hours
, for a one-way fare of about
. You can also transfer via Olongapo.
From downtown San Antonio to Pundaquit beach is about
15–20 minutes
, for a charter fare of about
per vehicle.
Rent a banca through a boat association or resort at Pundaquit beach. A round trip to Nagsasa alone on a small boat (up to 4 people) runs about
, while a hopping trip covering the islands and Anawangin runs about
, with fares rising for larger boats and groups.
If staying overnight, agree precisely on a pickup time for the next day and get the boat captain's contact number. Overnight packages bundling camping gear and the boat (about
per person, varying by group size) are also common.
Take NLEX and SCTEX to the Tipo exit, then pass through Subic and Olongapo before heading north along the Zambales coastal road. It's about
4–5 hours
from Manila to Pundaquit, and you can find paid parking with a local household or resort in Pundaquit.
If coming from Korea, Clark International Airport (CRK) is closest. It's about
2–3 hours
from the airport by car via Olongapo to San Antonio; by public transport, take a bus from a terminal near Clark to Olongapo, then transfer to a bus bound for Iba.
The dry season,
November–May
, is best.
December–February
sees nighttime temperatures drop to around
, comfortable for sleeping in a tent, and
March–May
has the calmest sea and warmest water, good for swimming. That said, the campsite gets crowded on summer-break and Holy Week weekends, so choose a weekday.
In the wet season,
June–October

, the southwest monsoon (Habagat) blows straight in off the sea, raising waves, and the coast guard often halts small-boat trips. Waterfall flow peaks just after this period, but the swollen stream can make trekking dangerous, so visiting near the end of the wet season, in
November
, gives you a good chance at both a fuller waterfall and a calm sea. Right after a typhoon passes, driftwood and debris sometimes pile up on the beach.

Tent camping is the standard at Nagsasa, and each campsite has wooden huts and rental tents. Many places only offer solar-powered lighting, and it's customary to keep quiet from around 10 PM. A few campsites run simple rooms, but there are few of them, so book ahead in peak season. For more comfort, stay at a beach resort in Pundaquit (about
per night) and visit as a day-trip hop.

There's almost no restaurant inside Nagsasa — the shop sells only instant noodles, snacks, and drinks. It's common to buy rice, meat and fish to grill, fruit, and ice at the market in Pundaquit or San Antonio and bring it in a cooler; overnight packages sometimes include charcoal and cooking equipment as well. Zambales is famous across the Philippines for its sweet mangoes, so during mango season,
April–May
, be sure to try carabao mangoes from San Antonio market.
San Antonio and Pundaquit have few ATMs. Bring enough cash to cover the boat, entrance fees, and food.
Phone signal barely reaches here. Let family know your schedule and return time in advance.
Bring a power bank, a headlamp, and plenty of spare batteries. Don't count on being able to charge anything.
Bring at least 3 liters of drinking water per person per day. Campsite pump water is for washing only.
Some campsites collect a trash deposit. Bring large trash bags and carry all your garbage back out.
For the waterfall trek and hill climb, trekking sandals you don't mind getting wet work well — you'll cross the stream several times and the rocks are slippery.
Fine sand blows into your tent when the wind picks up. Bring long stakes for sand and a waterproof groundsheet.
Renting a boat through a registered boat association or resort helps avoid problems with pickup times not being honored.

Missing the first pre-dawn bus delays your arrival in Pundaquit, and afternoon waves can make it hard to depart by boat. Arriving in San Antonio or Pundaquit the night before, staying over, and heading out early the next morning is also a good approach.
Wind picks up and waves rise in the afternoon. Take the return boat before noon if possible, and don't push to go out on a day the coast guard has halted departures.
In some spots, the water deepens just a few steps from shore, and there are no lifeguards. Children and weak swimmers should wear a life vest.
The stream to the falls can rise suddenly after rain. Follow your guide if they tell you to stop.
The sand and grassy hill have no shade at midday and get very hot. Guard against heatstroke and sunburn.
Only build fires and cook in designated spots. The dry agoho forest and grass catch fire easily.
There have been cases of belongings going missing at campsites. Keep valuables on you or leave them at home.
